coherence.reasons: Both run a clean pyramid from governing thought to slides. X is the tighter line: cost, limits, options, plan, with each section title restating an executive-summary claim. Its one slip is calling Option K the 'only design' that passes the service, capacity, budget and reversibility tests, when its own table rates keeping East as today as 'safe'. Y is more complete in separating the two closure variants (Central 'breaks' the tests, cross-dock 'cannot yet prove' them) and carries that distinction through every test. Its slips are some repetition across the cross-dock slides and a title saying waiting beats closing 'even under Reading B' when its own sum shows closing gains $0.14M over two years on that reading. These offset; the difference is negligible.

judgment.reasons: Both land on the key's preferred answer: keep East, take Option K, test the cross-dock, decide at the 2029 lease end, and drop full consolidation. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It defines the deferral path as its own option and costs the test (capped at $0.25M, flagged as an assumption needing provider agreement and no two-year minimum). It sets explicit gate criteria: at least 92% all-ZIP over the test, at least 90% in peak weeks, a network rate of 93.5%, and cost at least $0.2M a year below K. It adds a guardrail on Option K itself (East all-ZIP rate at or above 95%, since shift changes could hurt service) and checks that East can handle 220k orders. It also tests whether closing now would pay under the favourable fee reading. X has a good threshold table and spots the same fee-versus-floor question, but its cross-dock test is unfunded and unstructured, it sets no pass/fail criteria for the 2028 decision, and it does not consider that Option K could affect service.

evidence.reasons: Both get all four required calculations right: $1.20M of added cost, $0.10M net saving, 389,600 against 360,000, and 90.3% network service. Both derive the 88.3% Eastern threshold, correct the 98% versus 96% figure, treat the renewal claim as confounded, and discount the pilot. I checked the arithmetic in both and found no numerical errors. X's figures hold ($2.6M / $2.8M / $2.9M / $3.05M, the 50-cent surcharge, the $8.75 break-even, the −$650K two-year result). Y's full network cost model, two-year totals, volume break-evens (160k, 220k, 50k, 150k), the 8,600 late orders and the Reading B sums also hold. Y uses the evidence somewhat further: it sizes the lower-growth case the pack asks for (374.8k, still over capacity), notes that the measurement basis of the 84% and 93% is unstated, and labels its own assumptions as such. X has small overreaches: the 'only design' claim, and 'payback runs past 2029' at zero damage when 2.5 years lands in mid-2029.

revision.reasons: The key expects the CEO's view to be kept with conditions. Y tests it explicitly, breaking it into five sub-claims with verdicts, and refines it in three ways: optimize rather than merely retain; capacity rules out only consolidation into Central, not the cross-dock, which fails on cost and unproven service instead; and keep East through 2029 rather than permanently, with a gate. It also notes that the corrections cut both ways, weakening the service and loyalty case for East as well as the saving. X reaches the same conditional keep and does show that K is the cheapest compliant design, which was the CEO's unproven point. But it never engages the hypothesis as such, and does not point out that the CEO's capacity rationale does not apply to the cross-dock option.

overall.reasons: Both are sound, numerically accurate and reach the same defensible recommendation, and X is the more economical read. Y would serve the board better because it turns the middle path into something executable: a costed test, quantified gate criteria, guardrails on Option K, a sized lower-growth case and four specific decisions requested today. It also tests the CEO's hypothesis openly and separates which constraint defeats which closure variant. X leaves the cross-dock test and the 2028 decision criteria underspecified.
